claims.text: Adding zirconium to a multicomponent alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Zirconium addition increases atomic packing frustration.
Zirconium addition slows atomic mobility in the alloy.
Increased packing frustration and slower atomic mobility suppress nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling.
An AlNbTiVZr-type alloy is an example of the proposed zirconium-containing multicomponent alloy.
The zirconium-containing alloy can be processed from the melt under an inert argon atmosphere.
Rapid quenching can bypass crystallization in both the zirconium-containing alloy and the zirconium-free control.
Zirconium has a larger atomic radius than the other constituent elements in the proposed alloy.
The larger zirconium radius increases atomic-level packing disorder and local strain fields.
Zirconium-induced atomic-size mismatch disrupts long-range periodicity.
Zirconium-induced atomic-size mismatch retards atomic diffusion.
The resulting disorder destabilizes crystal-nucleus formation and favors vitrification.
The zirconium-containing alloy will have a larger critical casting thickness for amorphous-structure formation than the zirconium-free baseline.
The zirconium-containing alloy will have a lower crystallization-onset temperature during controlled heating than the zirconium-free baseline.
The appropriate baseline is the same multicomponent alloy processed identically but without zirconium.
Excessive zirconium may cause phase separation or crystallization.
An insufficient cooling rate may cause crystallization.
The effect of zirconium on glass-forming ability depends on the other alloying elements and their atomic-size differences.
Zirconium is known to enhance glass-forming ability in many alloy systems through size mismatch and kinetic slowing.
The quantitative improvement and optimal zirconium concentration in high-entropy or similar multicomponent alloys remain undetermined.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says zirconium retards diffusion and destabilizes crystal-nucleus formation, but the predicted outcome includes a lower crystallization-onset temperature during heating, which implies crystallization begins at a lower temperature. No explanation reconciles these statements.
